channel.title: AgentSee Podcast
channel.description: James Hartt and Abrar Mahmood are building a software agency from the ground up, in public, with agents doing the work. Every agency was organised around one scarce thing, engineering time, and that constraint has moved. Each episode is what they actually did, what it cost, what broke, and which of their stated questions it touched.
channel.itunes:author: AgentSee

item.title: Twenty questions before you build
item.itunes:title: Twenty questions before you build
item.description:
James and Abrar go through the twenty questions before you build, a group of four at a time: the idea, the care a domain needs, the conditions it runs in, its shape, and who owns it once it exists. Code is a byproduct now, so the questions are where the thinking goes; a regulator changes the build and keeping up with one is work of its own; scale that never arrives slows you down and scale that does sets fire to things; offline is the requirement that arrives at the eleventh hour; and somebody has to be able to restore the backup. It ends with the brief, the things they insist on for every build, and a flood of CVEs.

Chapters:

  • 00:00 A toy from the playground, and twenty questions
  • 01:59 Where it came from: code as a byproduct
  • 03:36 The idea: what should it do, and for whom
  • 06:59 Care needed: the regulator, and keeping up with it
  • 11:35 Running conditions: the busiest day, uptime, platforms
  • 16:01 Offline, the requirement that arrives at the eleventh hour
  • 20:37 Shape: AI inside it, how often it changes, what must never happen
  • 25:04 What an offline flow looks like: pen and paper
  • 26:36 Owning it: worth it, signed off, and looked after by whom
  • 30:57 The brief, and what we always insist on
  • 32:15 Security: a flood of CVEs, and vibe-coded targets
  • 33:55 A small team that can do what a giant one could
  • 35:54 Wrap: a bit of whimsy, and guests from here on
  • 36:51 Outro

Mentioned:

  • Issue No. 7: Twenty questions, and the one that counted was the twenty-first
  • The twenty questions, to run in your own assistant
  • The skill file itself, in the open
  • CVE, the vulnerability catalogue the flood lands in

Of the questions on the site, this one touches:

  • 1. If writing the code is no longer the expensive part, what is the client actually buying?
  • 3. What is a product manager when the specification is executable?
  • 4. Who is accountable for a system that nobody typed?
  • 5. How do you run acceptance testing on something produced faster than a person can read it?

item.title: Vibe coding, and the rise of the product engineer
item.itunes:title: Vibe coding, and the rise of the product engineer
item.description:
Abrar builds GradeDrive, an AI marking tool for schools, with a non-technical co-founder, and helps a second startup where the product team ships its own ideas. He explains what makes that safe: a skill that gives every idea its own worktree, database and dev server, a read-only environment the agent can be trusted with, guidelines written after a feature that ran a whole class's PDF in the browser, and a draft pull request that spins up an environment of its own. James asks about native apps, things going off the rails and what the job is now. The answers: web is easy and native is not, it is easier than ever to build sloppy stuff, taste still comes from people, and Abrar has not opened a code editor in six months.

Chapters:

  • 00:00 GradeDrive, and another startup
  • 01:36 How it used to work: idea, engineer, ticket, wait
  • 04:10 Vibe coding: quick, motivating, throwaway
  • 07:15 Prototypes that carry the intent
  • 10:28 Enablement: a read-only environment, a worktree per idea
  • 14:43 When a vibed feature went wrong
  • 19:00 Agents that check their own work in a browser
  • 21:42 Web is easy, native is not
  • 26:25 One-shotting a feature, and the draft pull request
  • 30:06 Easier than ever to build sloppy stuff
  • 34:43 Engineering is enablement; then gravitate to product
  • 37:40 Coding is an abstraction; taste is still ours
  • 42:11 The role is exhausting: the thinking comes first
  • 47:34 Where people hit the wall
  • 52:10 Outro

  • Claude Code, and the Claude desktop app the co-founder uses

  • 7. What does taste mean when volume is free?
  • 8. Do engineers still want the job? What is it now — author, reviewer, director, or something we don't yet have a word for?

item.title: Running our own mail server, on purpose
item.itunes:title: Running our own mail server, on purpose
item.description:
James set up AgentSee's own mail server on a Swiss VPS, with an agent writing the OpenTofu and most of the configuration: two afternoons' work rather than the weeks it would once have taken. Abrar asks what was hard, and the answer is the click ops inside Stalwart's admin panel, a CLI that was not built for an agent, buttons the model insisted existed, and making the result reproducible afterwards with a snapshot script. They also cover borrowing sender reputation, the monitoring that is not built yet, whether either of them would recommend this to a client (no), and what it is like to let an agent drive the browser.

  • 00:00 Why mail at all
  • 02:15 The alternatives, and why Infomaniak

item.title: Introductions and the premise
item.itunes:title: Introductions and the premise
item.description:
James Hartt and Abrar Mahmood introduce themselves and the premise of AgentSee: a software agency for a world where working software can be prompted into existence. Agencies were organised around protecting developer time and billing for it; when that is no longer the expensive part, what does a client pay for? Their answer, for now, is the last stretch to production, which is as hard as it ever was.
